title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the 21st Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: 1. Where the countries of the parties to an international sale of goods contract are all Contracting States to the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG), the provisions of the Convention shall apply preferentially; matters not covered by the Convention shall be governed by the law chosen in the contract. Where the parties to an international sale of goods contract expressly exclude the application of the CISG, the Convention shall not apply. 2. In an international sale of goods contract, even if the goods delivered by the seller are defective, as long as the buyer can use or resell the goods after making reasonable efforts, such defect shall not be deemed to constitute a fundamental breach under the CISG.
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on the Release of the 21st Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2019] No. 3

To: High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and approval by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the six cases including the dispute over an international sale of goods contract between Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. and ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH (Guiding Cases No. 107-112) are hereby released as the 21st batch of guiding cases for reference in the adjudication of similar cases.

February 25, 2019

Guiding Case No. 107

Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH

— Dispute over an international sale of goods contract

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on February 25, 2019)

Keywords: Civil / International sale of goods contract / United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods / Application of law / Fundamental breach

Ruling Gist

1. Where the countries of the parties to an international sale of goods contract are all Contracting States to the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, the provisions of the Convention shall prevail in application; for matters not covered by the Convention, the law chosen by the parties in the contract shall apply. If the parties to an international sale of goods contract expressly exclude the application of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, the Convention shall not apply.

2. In an international sale of goods contract, if the goods delivered by the seller are defective, but the buyer can use or resell the goods after reasonable efforts, such defects shall not be deemed to constitute a fundamental breach as stipulated by the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods.

Related Laws

Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China

Articles 1 and 25 of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods

Basic Facts

On April 11, 2008, Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sinochem Singapore) and ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH (hereinafter referred to as German Krupp) signed a Procurement Contract for the purchase of petroleum coke, stipulating that the contract shall be made, governed, and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, USA, then in force. Sinochem Singapore paid the full price as agreed, but the HGI index of the petroleum coke delivered by German Krupp was only 32, which did not comply with the typical HGI index range of 36-46 agreed in the contract. Sinochem Singapore considered that German Krupp's actions constituted a fundamental breach and requested the rescission of the contract, the return of the purchase price, and compensation for losses.

Judgment

The High People's Court of Jiangsu Province held at first instance that, according to the relevant provisions of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, the HGI index of the petroleum coke provided by German Krupp was far lower than the contractually agreed standard, making it difficult to sell the petroleum coke in the domestic market, thus the expected purpose of signing the contract could not be achieved. Therefore, German Krupp's actions constituted a fundamental breach. On December 19, 2012, the High People's Court of Jiangsu Province rendered the civil judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004: 1. Declared the Procurement Contract signed between ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH and Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. on April 11, 2008, void. 2. Ordered ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH to refund the purchase price of USD 2,684,302.90 to Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, and to pay interest from September 25, 2008, to the date of payment determined by this judgment. 3. Ordered ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH to compensate Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. for losses of USD 520,339.77 within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment.

After the judgment was pronounced, German Krupp, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Supreme People's Court, arguing that the application of law in the first-instance judgment was erroneous. The Supreme People's Court held that the facts found in the first-instance judgment were basically clear, but there were errors in the application of law and improper determination of liability, which should be corrected. On June 30, 2014, the Supreme People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2013) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 35: 1. Set aside Item 1 of the civil judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004 of the High People's Court of Jiangsu Province. 2. Changed Item 2 of the civil judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004 of the High People's Court of Jiangsu Province to: ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH shall compensate Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. for the loss of purchase price of USD 1,610,581.74 within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, and pay interest from September 25, 2008, to the date of payment determined by this judgment. 3. Changed Item 3 of the civil judgment (2009) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 0004 of the High People's Court of Jiangsu Province to: ThyssenKrupp Metallurgical Products GmbH shall compensate Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. for storage loss of USD 98,442.79 within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment. 4. Dismissed the other claims of Sinochem International (Singapore) Pte. Ltd.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that this case is a dispute over an international sale of goods contract, with both parties being foreign companies, thus the case has foreign-related elements. Article 2 of the Interpretation (I) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations stipulates: "For foreign-related civil relations that occurred before the implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, the people's court shall determine the applicable law according to the relevant legal provisions in effect at the time of the occurrence of the foreign-related civil relation; if no such laws existed at that time, the provisions of the Law on Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations may be consulted for determination." The Procurement Contract in question was signed on April 11, 2008, before the implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations. At the time the parties signed the contract, Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provided: "The parties to a foreign-related contract may choose the law applicable to the resolution of contractual disputes, unless otherwise provided by law. If the parties to a foreign-related contract have made no choice, the law of the country with the closest connection to the contract shall apply." The parties in this case agreed in the contract that it shall be made, governed, and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, USA, then in force. This agreement does not violate legal provisions and should be deemed valid. Since Singapore and Germany, the countries where the parties' places of business are located, are both Contracting States to the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, and the United States is also a Contracting State to that Convention, and during the first-instance trial the parties jointly agreed to apply the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods as the basis for determining their rights and obligations, without excluding the application of the Convention, the High People's Court of Jiangsu Province correctly applied the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods to this case. For issues arising in the trial that are not covered by the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, the law of the State of New York, as chosen by the parties, shall apply. The "Digest of Case Law on the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods" is not a part of the Convention and cannot be used as the legal basis for adjudicating this case. However, it can be used as appropriate reference material for accurately understanding the meaning of the relevant provisions of the Convention.

The typical HGI index of the petroleum coke agreed by the parties in the Procurement Contract was between 36-46, but the HGI index of the petroleum coke actually delivered by German Krupp was 32, lower than the minimum typical HGI index agreed, thus it did not comply with the contract. The High People's Court of Jiangsu Province correctly found that German Krupp constituted a breach of contract.

Regarding whether the above breach by German Krupp constitutes a fundamental breach: First, looking at the content of the specifications agreed in the contract regarding the chemical and physical properties that the petroleum coke must meet, the contract set out seven aspects: moisture content, sulfur content, ash content, volatile matter content, size, calorific value, and hardness (HGI value). From the facts, Sinochem Singapore only considered that the HGI index did not comply with the contract, and raised no objection to the other six indicators. Based on the witness testimony submitted by the parties and the statements of witnesses in court, the HGI index represents the grindability index of petroleum coke; the lower the index, the harder the petroleum coke and the more difficult it is to grind. However, the explanation provided by the School of Materials Science and Engineering of Shanghai University, submitted by Sinochem Singapore, does not deny that petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 can be used, but merely states that its uses are limited. Therefore, it can be determined that although the HGI index of the petroleum coke in question did not comply with the contract, the batch of petroleum coke still has utility value. Second, during the first-instance trial, Sinochem Singapore made active efforts to resell the petroleum coke in question to minimize losses, and stated in correspondence to German Krupp regarding related issues that the resale price of the petroleum coke was "not lower than the reasonable market price." This fact indicates that the petroleum coke in question could be sold at a reasonable price. Third, considering the understanding of the fundamental breach clause of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods in the judgments of other countries, as long as the buyer can use or resell the goods after reasonable efforts, even at a discount, the lack of conformity still does not constitute a fundamental breach. Therefore, German Krupp's delivery of petroleum coke with an HGI index of 32 should not be deemed a fundamental breach. The High People's Court of Jiangsu Province's determination that German Krupp constituted a fundamental breach and its judgment declaring the Procurement Contract void constituted an error in the application of law and should be corrected.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Ren Xuefeng, Cheng Mingzhu, Zhu Ke)

Guiding Case No. 108

Zhejiang Longda Stainless Steel Co., Ltd. v. A.P. Moller-Maersk A/S

— Dispute over a contract for carriage of goods by sea

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on February 25, 2019)

Keywords: Civil / Contract for carriage of goods by sea / Modification of contract / Change of port / Return of cargo / Right of defense

Ruling Gist

In a contract for carriage of goods by sea, according to the provisions of Article 308 of the Contract Law, before the carrier delivers the goods to the consignee, the consignor has the right to request modification of the transport contract. However, both parties must still determine their respective rights and obligations in accordance with the principle of fairness stipulated in Article 5 of the Contract Law. When the consignor exercises this right, the carrier may also correspondingly exercise a certain right of defense. If modifying the contract for carriage of goods by sea is difficult to achieve or would seriously affect the carrier's normal operations, the carrier may refuse the consignor's request to change the port or return the cargo, but shall promptly notify the consignor of the reason for the inability to change.

Related Laws

Article 308 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Article 86 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

In June 2014, Zhejiang Longda Stainless Steel Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Longda Company) exported a batch of stainless steel seamless products from Ningbo Port, China, to Colombo Port, Sri Lanka, with a declared customs value of USD 366,918.97. Longda Company booked space with A.P. Moller-Maersk A/S (hereinafter referred to as Maersk Company) through a freight forwarder. The goods in question were loaded into 4 containers and shipped on June 28, 2014, with Longda Company requesting telex release at the time of shipment. On July 9, 2014, Longda Company sent an email to Maersk Company via the freight forwarder, stating that the goods had been shipped to the wrong destination and requesting a change of port or return. Maersk Company replied the same day, stating that since the goods were less than 2 days away from the destination port, a change of port could not be arranged, and if return was required, confirmation from the destination port would be needed before responding. The next day, the freight forwarder for Longda Company inquired whether the goods could be returned on the same vessel. Maersk Company replied the same day, stating "Return on the same vessel is not feasible. After the goods are discharged at the destination port, the current consignee needs to clear customs at the destination port and then apply to the local customs for return. Only after customs approval can the return arrangements be made." On July 10, 2014, Longda Company further asked, "This shipment needs to be returned because customs clearance cannot be completed; that's why we want to return it to Ningbo. Is there any other way?" Thereafter, Maersk Company did not reply further.

The goods in question arrived at the destination port around July 12, 2014. At Longda Company's request, Maersk Company issued a full set of original bills of lading numbered 603 386 880 on January 29, 2015. According to the bill of lading, the consignor was Longda Company, the consignee and notify party were both VENUS STEEL PVT LTD, the port of loading was Ningbo, China, and the port of discharge was Colombo. On May 19, 2015, Longda Company sent an email to Maersk Company stating that it had applied for return as requested by Maersk Company. Maersk Company then informed Longda Company that the goods in question had been auctioned.

Judgment

The Ningbo Maritime Court rendered the civil judgment (2015) Yong Hai Fa Shang Chu Zi No. 534 on March 4, 2016, holding that Longda Company failed to take effective measures such as taking delivery of the goods itself, resulting in the goods being auctioned by customs, and the risk of loss should be borne by Longda Company, thus dismissing Longda Company's claims. After the first-instance judgment, Longda Company appealed. The High People's Court of Zhejiang Province rendered the civil judgment (2016) Zhe Min Zhong Zi No. 222 on September 29, 2016, setting aside the first-instance judgment and ordering Maersk Company to compensate Longda Company for the loss of goods of USD 183,459.49 and interest within ten days from the date of service of the judgment. The court of second instance held that, pursuant to Article 308 of the Contract Law, Longda Company had the right to request a change of port or return before Maersk Company delivered the goods. After Longda Company made the request for return, Maersk Company neither clearly refused to arrange the return nor notified Longda Company to handle the matter itself, and should bear corresponding compensation liability for the loss of the goods, with the liability ratio determined at 50%. Dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, Maersk Company applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2017) Zui Gao Fa Min Zai No. 412 on December 29, 2017, setting aside the second-instance judgment and affirming the first-instance judgment.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that the provisions of the Contract Law and the Maritime Code regulating maritime transport relations and ship relations are ordinary law and special law, respectively. According to Article 89 of the Maritime Code, before the voyage commences at the port of loading, the consignor may demand the rescission of the contract. In this case, Longda Company requested the carrier to return the cargo or change the port during the sea transport. Since the Maritime Code does not provide for the consignor's right to request modification of the transport contract during the voyage, Article 308 of the Contract Law, which governs the consignor's right to request modification of the transport contract, may apply to this case. Based on the fundamental principle that special law prevails over ordinary law, Article 308 of the Contract Law, which regulates general transport contracts, when applied to contracts for carriage of goods by sea, should be limited by the basic value orientation and mandatory provisions of the Maritime Code. The consignor's exercise of the right to modify the transport contract under Article 308 of the Contract Law shall not cause a manifest imbalance of interests among the parties to the contract for carriage of goods by sea, nor shall it cause the carrier to breach its obligations to arrange reasonable routes owed to other consignors, or deprive the carrier of its corresponding right of defense regarding modifications to the performance of the contract for carriage of goods by sea.

The general principles stipulated in the General Provisions of the Contract Law are the legislative criteria of the Contract Law, applicable to all areas of the Contract Law, and serve as the basis for specific systems and norms of the Contract Law. Under Article 308 of the Contract Law, before the carrier delivers the goods to the consignee, the consignor has the right to request modification of the transport contract. However, both parties must still determine their rights and obligations in accordance with the principle of fairness stipulated in Article 5 of the Contract Law. The carriage of goods by sea has particularities such as large volumes, predetermined voyages, and relatively fixed routes. The consignor's request to change the port or return the cargo is often not only difficult to implement but may also impede the carrier's normal operations or cause substantial harm to other consignors or consignees. Under such circumstances, requiring the carrier to unconditionally comply with the consignor's request to modify the transport contract would be manifestly unfair. Therefore, under a contract for carriage of goods by sea, the consignor cannot exercise the right to request modification without limitation, and the carrier is not required to unconditionally comply with the consignor's instructions for modification in all circumstances. To reasonably balance the interests of the parties in a contract for carriage of goods by sea, while the consignor exercises the right to request modification, the carrier correspondingly enjoys a certain right of defense. If modifying the transport contract is difficult to achieve or would seriously affect the carrier's normal operations, the carrier may refuse the consignor's request to change the port or return the cargo, but shall promptly notify the consignor of the reason for the inability to execute. If the carrier's defense regarding the reason for inability to execute is established, the carrier's failure to follow the consignor's instructions for return or change of port is not improper.

The goods in this case were carried on an international liner service. The carrying vessel carried numerous containers belonging to other cargo owners in addition to the 4 containers consigned by Longda Company. The goods were loaded and shipped on June 28, 2014, and arrived at the destination port around July 12, 2014. It was not until July 9, 2014, that Longda Company requested Maersk Company to return the cargo or change the port. By that time, the voyage was mostly completed, with only two or three days remaining until arrival at the destination port. Maersk Company's defenses that a change of port could not be arranged due to the voyage and that return on the same vessel was not feasible were consistent with the facts of the case. These defenses were established, and Maersk Company's failure to arrange return or change of port was not improper.

Maersk transported the cargo to the port of destination. Because no one claimed the cargo, Maersk's unloading of the cargo onto the dock at the port of destination complies with the provisions of Article 86 of the Maritime Code. On July 9, 2014, Maersk replied to Longda by email that the arrival at the port of destination was less than two days away. Longda was aware of the approximate time of the cargo's arrival at the port and knew that no one would claim the cargo at the port of destination, yet it took no measures to deal with the cargo over a period of eight months, resulting in the cargo being auctioned by Customs. Although Longda claimed that Maersk failed to fulfill its duty of care in handling the cargo, it did not provide evidence to prove that Maersk had improperly handled the cargo. Longda's claim lacks a basis. According to Article 86 of the Maritime Code, the expenses and risks arising after Maersk unloaded the cargo shall be borne by the consignee, and Maersk, as the carrier, does not need to bear the corresponding risks.

(Judges of the final judgment: Wang Shumei, Yu Xiaohan, Huang Xiwu)

Guiding Case No. 109

Anhui Foreign Economic Construction (Group) Co., Ltd. v.
Oriental Real Estate Co., Ltd. — dispute over guarantee fraud

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court and released on February 25, 2019)

Keywords: civil/guarantee fraud/review of underlying transaction/principle of limited and necessary/independent counter-guarantee

Ruling Gist

1. When determining whether fraud exists in an independent guarantee, a review of the underlying transaction shall adhere to the principle of limited and necessary review. The scope of review shall be limited to whether the beneficiary clearly knew that the counterparty to the underlying contract was not in default of the underlying contract, and whether the beneficiary clearly knew that it had no right to demand payment.

2. A beneficiary's default under the underlying contract does not affect its right to present documents in accordance with the terms of the independent guarantee and demand payment.

3. When determining whether fraud exists under an independent counter-guarantee, even if fraud exists in the independent guarantee, the People's Court shall not issue an order to suspend payment under the independent counter-guarantee if payment has already been made in good faith under the independent guarantee.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 8 and Article 44 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations

Basic Facts

On January 16, 2010, Oriental Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Oriental Real Estate), as the developer, signed the "Construction Contract for the Lakefront Chinese Mansion Project in Costa Rica" (hereinafter referred to as the "Construction Contract") with Anhui Foreign Economic Construction (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Foreign Economic Group), as the contractor, and Anhui Foreign Economic Construction Central America Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Foreign Economic Central America), as the builder, in San Jose, Republic of Costa Rica. The contract stipulated that the contractor would construct three 14-story mixed-use commercial and residential buildings. On May 26, 2010, Foreign Economic Group applied to China Construction Bank Corporation Anhui Branch (hereinafter referred to as CCB Anhui Branch) and, with Banco de Costa Rica as the issuing bank, opened a performance guarantee in favor of Oriental Real Estate, with the guarantee matter being the Lakefront Chinese Mansion Project in Costa Rica. On May 28, 2010, Banco de Costa Rica issued Performance Guarantee No. G051225, with the guarantor being CCB Anhui Branch, the principal being Foreign Economic Group, the beneficiary being Oriental Real Estate, the guaranteed amount being USD 2,008,000, and the validity period until October 12, 2011, later extended to February 12, 2012. The guarantee stated: an unconditional, irrevocable, mandatory, demand guarantee. To execute this guarantee, the beneficiary is required to submit duplicate copies of supporting documents to the Foreign Trade Department of the Central Office of Banco de Costa Rica, indicating the reasons for executing the guarantee, in addition to a notarized declaration by the beneficiary stating the date on which Foreign Economic Central America was notified of the claim due to default, accompanied by the original guarantee certificate and any amendments already issued. CCB Anhui Branch also issued a counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289 to Banco de Costa Rica, undertaking to pay the amount under the guarantee within twenty days of receiving notification from Banco de Costa Rica. The counter-guarantee was "unconditional, irrevocable, and payable on demand" and stipulated compliance with the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (ICC Publication No. 458).

During the performance of the Construction Contract, on January 23, 2012, architects Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora issued a "Project Inspection Report." The report identified defects in the construction project such as "poor workmanship," "low quality," and the need for modification or repair. On February 7, 2012, Foreign Economic Central America filed an arbitration request with the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers against Oriental Real Estate as the respondent, alleging that Oriental Real Estate was in arrears in paying the project progress payments for the completed work and corresponding interest, and requested rescission of the contract and an award of damages. On February 8, 2012, Oriental Real Estate submitted to Banco de Costa Rica a claim statement, notice of default, declaration of default, the Project Inspection Report, and other guarantee cashing documents, demanding execution of the guarantee. On February 10, 2012, Banco de Costa Rica sent a telex to CCB Anhui Branch stating that Oriental Real Estate had filed a claim demanding payment of USD 2,008,000 under Bank Guarantee No. G051225, and Banco de Costa Rica further required CCB Anhui Branch to pay the said amount by February 16, 2012. On February 12, 2012, upon the application of Foreign Economic Central America, the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of the Republic of Costa Rica issued an interim protective measure injunction, ordering Banco de Costa Rica to suspend the execution of Performance Guarantee No. G051225.

On February 23, 2012, Foreign Economic Group filed a lawsuit with the Hefei Intermediate People's Court on the dispute over guarantee fraud, and simultaneously applied for suspension of payment under Guarantee No. G051225 and Guarantee No. 34147020000289. On February 27, 2012, the first-instance court issued an order (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005-1, ruling to suspend payment under Guarantee No. G051225 and Guarantee No. 34147020000289, and on February 28, 2012, served the above order on CCB Anhui Branch. On February 29, 2012, CCB Anhui Branch sent a telex to Banco de Costa Rica informing it of the order made by the first-instance court, and on the same day sent a copy of the order to Banco de Costa Rica, which received the copy of the order on March 5, 2012.

On March 6, 2012, the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of the Republic of Costa Rica ruled against Foreign Economic Central America's application for preventive measures, lifting the interim protective measure injunction. On March 20, 2012, at the request of Banco de Costa Rica, CCB Anhui Branch extended the validity period of Guarantee No. 34147020000289. On March 21, 2012, Banco de Costa Rica paid the amount under Guarantee No. G051225 to Oriental Real Estate.

On July 9, 2013, the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers rendered an arbitral award. The arbitral award found that Oriental Real Estate had materially breached the Construction Contract during its performance, and ruled to terminate the Construction Contract, ordering Oriental Real Estate to pay Foreign Economic Central America a total of USD 800,058.45 for progress payments No. 1 to No. 18, plus interest. The claim for payment for progress No. 19 was not supported because the developer had not accepted the work. As the amount under Guarantee No. G051225 had already been paid, the request of Foreign Economic Central America for return of the guarantee was not supported.

Judgment

On April 9, 2014, the Hefei Intermediate People's Court of Anhui Province rendered civil judgment (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005: 1. The claim of Oriental Real Estate under Performance Guarantee No. G051225 constituted fraud; 2. CCB Anhui Branch shall terminate payment of USD 2,008,000 under Bank Guarantee No. 34147020000289 to Banco de Costa Rica; 3. All other claims of Foreign Economic Group were dismissed. Oriental Real Estate, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed. On March 19, 2015, the Anhui High People's Court rendered civil judgment (2014) Wan Min Er Zhong Zi No. 00389: dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. Oriental Real Estate, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. On December 14, 2017, the Supreme People's Court rendered civil judgment (2017) Zui Gao Fa Min Zai No. 134: 1. Setting aside the civil judgments of the Anhui High People's Court (2014) Wan Min Er Zhong Zi No. 00389 and the Hefei Intermediate People's Court of Anhui Province (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005; 2. Dismissing the claims of Foreign Economic Group.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held:

First, regarding the identification basis, jurisdiction, and applicable law for the case involving independent guarantee fraud. The habitual residence of the disputing parties, Oriental Real Estate and Banco de Costa Rica, is outside the territory of China, making this a foreign-related commercial dispute. According to Article 8 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations: "The characterization of foreign-related civil relations shall be governed by the law of the forum." Foreign Economic Group, as the domestic parent company of Foreign Economic Central America, is the applicant for the guarantee in question. It applied to CCB Anhui Branch to issue an on-demand counter-guarantee to Banco de Costa Rica, which in turn issued a performance guarantee to the beneficiary, Oriental Real Estate. According to the text of the guarantee, the payment obligations of Banco de Costa Rica and CCB Anhui Branch are independent of the underlying transaction and the guarantee application relationship. Therefore, the above guarantee can be identified as an on-demand independent guarantee, and the above counter-guarantee can be identified as an on-demand independent counter-guarantee. Foreign Economic Group brought this lawsuit to the first-instance court on the ground of guarantee fraud. The nature of this case is a guarantee fraud dispute. The independent counter-guarantee sought to be suspended was issued by CCB Anhui Branch, and the location of that branch shall be deemed the place of the alleged tortious result. The first-instance court, as the court of the place of the tort, has jurisdiction over this case. Because the guarantee in question specifies the application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees, it shall be determined that the content of those rules constitutes part of the disputed guarantee. According to Article 44 of the Law on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations: "Tort liability shall be governed by the law of the place where the tort is committed." The standard for determining guarantee fraud, which is not covered by the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees, shall be governed by the law of the People's Republic of China. China has not acceded to the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit, and the parties in this case did not agree to apply the Convention or incorporate its content as international trade rules into the guarantee. Based on the principle of party autonomy, the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit shall not apply.

Second, regarding whether the beneficiary, Oriental Real Estate, had prima facie evidence under the underlying contract to prove that its claim was factually based.

When a People's Court hears cases involving independent guarantees and counter-guarantees related to independent guarantees, its review of the underlying transaction shall adhere to the principles of limited review and necessary review. The scope of review shall be limited to whether the beneficiary clearly knew that the counterparty to the underlying contract was not in default of the underlying contract, or that there were no other facts leading to payment under the independent guarantee. Otherwise, a review of the underlying contract would undermine the institutional value of the "pay on first demand" nature of independent guarantees.

According to Article 68 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (For Trial Implementation), fraud is mainly manifested as fabrication of facts or concealment of the truth. Based on the facts found in the retrial, Banco de Costa Rica issued Performance Guarantee No. G051225, which clearly stipulated that the documents required to realize the guarantee were: supporting documents explaining the reason for executing the guarantee, the date of notifying Foreign Economic Central America of the request to execute the guarantee, the original guarantee certificate, and any amendments already issued. Foreign Economic Group claims that the conduct of Oriental Real Estate constitutes fraud under the independent guarantee. To do so, Foreign Economic Group must submit evidence proving that Oriental Real Estate, when realizing the independent guarantee, engaged in one of the following acts: 1. Submitting documents with false or forged content for the claim; 2. The claim completely lacks factual basis and credible support. In this case, the guarantee covered "the quality and durability of materials used during construction, compensation or indemnity for losses caused, and/or payment for the contractor's failure to perform its obligations." That is, the guarantee covered construction quality and other defaults. Therefore, the beneficiary only needs to submit prima facie evidence proving the existence of construction quality issues to satisfy the requirement of "supporting documents explaining the reason for executing the guarantee." During the performance of the underlying contract in this case, the project supervisors of Oriental Real Estate, Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora, issued a "Project Inspection Report" on January 23, 2012. The report identified defects such as "poor workmanship," "low quality," and the need for modification or repair. This "Project Inspection Report" constitutes prima facie evidence of the existence of construction quality issues.

The parties in this case did not explicitly stipulate in the Construction Contract or under the guarantee that the "Project Inspection Report" should be submitted to Banco de Costa Rica when realizing the guarantee. Therefore, Oriental Real Estate has the right to choose the type of "supporting documents explaining the reason for executing the guarantee" submitted to Banco de Costa Rica. Whether it submits the report to Banco de Costa Rica does not affect its right to realize the guarantee. Furthermore, neither the Construction Contract nor the guarantee stipulated that the above report must be issued by an AIA International Associate or a person with international membership in the American Institute of Architects. Therefore, whether Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora hold international membership in the American Institute of Architects does not affect their ability to issue the "Project Inspection Report" as the project supervisors for the developer. Foreign Economic Group was aware that both Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora were project supervisors for the developer. When it accepted the "Project Inspection Report" and received payment for the project, it recognized the supervisory capacity of Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora. It is logically inconsistent for Foreign Economic Group to now use evidence that it itself recognized to prove the supervisory capacity of Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora to argue that the "Project Inspection Report" issued by them is false. Because Foreign Economic Group failed to provide other evidence proving that Oriental Real Estate's realization of the guarantee in question completely lacked factual basis or that it submitted false or forged documents, Oriental Real Estate's application to Banco de Costa Rica to realize the guarantee rights has a factual basis.

In summary, the "Project Inspection Report" constitutes prima facie evidence of Foreign Economic Group's default under the underlying contract. The evidence provided by Foreign Economic Group is insufficient to prove that the above report is false or forged, nor is it sufficient to prove that Oriental Real Estate clearly knew that the counterparty to the underlying contract was not in default of the underlying contract, or that there were no other facts leading to payment under the independent guarantee, yet still demanded realization of the guarantee. Oriental Real Estate's realization of its rights under the independent guarantee, based on Foreign Economic Group's default under the underlying contract and in accordance with the contract terms, does not constitute guarantee fraud.

Third, regarding whether a beneficiary's default under the underlying contract of an independent guarantee necessarily constitutes fraudulent demand under the independent guarantee.

Foreign Economic Group argues that, according to Article 12, paragraphs (3), (4), and (5) of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Independent Guarantee Dispute Cases (hereinafter referred to as the Judicial Interpretation on Independent Guarantees), it should be determined that Oriental Real Estate constitutes independent guarantee fraud. According to Article 25 of the Judicial Interpretation on Independent Guarantees, after clarification in court, Foreign Economic Group still insisted that the handling of this case should not violate the spirit of the Judicial Interpretation on Independent Guarantees. In light of Foreign Economic Group's claims, the Supreme People's Court further elaborates on the relevant issues concerning the aforementioned Judicial Interpretation on Independent Guarantees.

An independent guarantee is independent of the underlying transaction between the principal and the beneficiary. The bank that issues the independent guarantee is only responsible for examining whether the documents submitted by the beneficiary comply with the terms of the guarantee and has the right to decide whether to pay. The guarantor bank's payment obligation is not affected by any defenses arising from the underlying transaction between the principal and the beneficiary. Oriental Real Estate, as the beneficiary, when submitting prima facie evidence of the existence of construction quality issues, even if it has not initiated any dispute resolution procedure such as litigation or arbitration, and the counterparty's default has not been confirmed through such procedures, this does not affect its right to realize the guarantee. Even if there are ongoing litigation or arbitration proceedings concerning the underlying contract, as long as the relevant dispute resolution procedure has not finally determined that the debtor under the underlying transaction has no payment or compensation liability, this does not affect the beneficiary's right to realize the guarantee. Furthermore, even if a final judgment or arbitral award finds that the beneficiary is in default under the underlying contract, the existence of such default does not necessarily constitute a sufficient and necessary condition for "fraud" in the guarantee.

In this case, the matters guaranteed by the letter of guarantee were the construction quality and other breaches of contract, and there was no logical causal relationship between the beneficiary's breach of failing to pay the project sum and the occurrence of quality issues in the project. Oriental Venture Company, as the beneficiary, its own breach in the performance of the underlying contract does not necessarily constitute fraudulent drawing under the independent letter of guarantee. Article 12, Paragraph 3 of the Judicial Interpretation on Independent Letters of Guarantee limits the condition for finding fraud in an independent letter of guarantee to "a court judgment or arbitral award determining that the debtor under the underlying transaction has no obligation to pay or bear liability." Therefore, unless otherwise agreed in the letter of guarantee, the review of the underlying contract should be limited to the performance matters within the scope of the guarantee. When considering whether the beneficiary's own breach in the underlying contract falls within the scope of fraud review for letters of guarantee, great caution should be exercised. Although the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers issued an arbitral award finding that Oriental Venture Company breached the contract during performance, the aforementioned arbitration proceedings were initiated by the Foreign Economic and Trade Group Company on February 7, 2012, and Oriental Venture Company did not file a counterclaim. The arbitral award made on July 9, 2013, only found Oriental Venture Company in breach regarding the claims of the Foreign Economic and Trade Group Company, but did not find that the Foreign Economic and Trade Group Company was exempted from payment or compensation liability due to the other party's breach. Therefore, it cannot be determined based on the content of the aforementioned arbitral award that Oriental Venture Company constituted fraud under the letter of guarantee as stipulated in Article 12, Paragraph 3 of the Judicial Interpretation on Independent Letters of Guarantee.

Furthermore, the fact of the dispute over project quality between the parties and the statements in the "Arbitral Award" from the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers concerning the project quality issues corroborate that the obligations of the Foreign Economic and Trade Central America Company under the "Construction Contract" were not fully performed. In this case, there was no situation where Oriental Venture Company confirmed that the underlying transaction debt had been fully performed or that the payment due event had not occurred. The existing evidence also cannot prove that Oriental Venture Company, knowing it had no right to demand payment, still abused that right. As the beneficiary, although Oriental Venture Company's breach in the performance of the underlying contract was confirmed by the arbitral award, it did not exempt the Foreign Economic and Trade Group Company from its payment or compensation liability. In summary, even applying the Judicial Interpretation on Independent Letters of Guarantee as argued by the Foreign Economic and Trade Group Company, the circumstances of this case do not constitute fraud under the letter of guarantee.

Fourth, concerning the issue of the independent counter-guarantee related to the independent letter of guarantee involved in this case.

Based on the characteristics of an independent letter of guarantee, the guarantor constitutes a direct payment obligation to the beneficiary separate from the debtor. There is no accessory nature of the right of defense between the independent letter of guarantee and the principal debt. Even if the debtor exercises its right of defense in a certain dispute resolution proceeding, it does not automatically entitle the independent guarantor to that defense benefit. Furthermore, even if there is a fraudulent drawing by the beneficiary under the independent letter of guarantee, it cannot be presumed that the guarantor bank constitutes a fraudulent drawing under the independent counter-guarantee. Only when the guarantor bank, knowing that the beneficiary's drawing is fraudulent and paying in violation of the principle of good faith, then claims payment from the counter-guarantor under the independent counter-guarantee, can the guarantor bank be found to have committed a fraudulent drawing under the independent counter-guarantee.

The Foreign Economic and Trade Group Company filed this lawsuit on the grounds of fraud under the letter of guarantee. It must provide evidence to prove that the Bank of Costa Rica, knowing that Oriental Venture Company was committing fraud under the independent letter of guarantee, still paid in violation of the principle of good faith, and then, as a beneficiary, made a demand for payment under the independent counter-guarantee payable on first demand, thereby constituting a fraudulent drawing under the counter-guarantee. Currently, the Foreign Economic and Trade Group Company not only fails to prove that the Bank of Costa Rica's payment to Oriental Venture Company under the independent letter of guarantee was fraudulent but also fails to present evidence proving that the Bank of Costa Rica's drawing under the independent counter-guarantee was fraudulent. Therefore, its claim for an injunction against payment under the independent counter-guarantee has no factual basis.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Chen Jizhong, Yang Honglei, Yang Xingye)

Guiding Case No. 110

Nanhai Rescue Bureau of the Ministry of Transport v.
Archangelos Investments Inc., and
Hong Kong Anda Ousen Co., Ltd., Shanghai Representative Office
— dispute over a marine salvage contract

(Discussed and approved by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on February 25, 2019)

Keywords: Civil / marine salvage contract / engaged salvage / salvage reward

Ruling Gist

1. Both the International Convention on Salvage 1989 and the Maritime Law of China stipulate the principle of "no cure, no pay" for salvage contracts, but both allow the parties to agree otherwise on the determination of the salvage reward. If the parties explicitly agree that the salved party shall pay the reward regardless of whether the salvage is successful, and the reward is calculated based on standards such as the horsepower-hour of the salvage vessel and the manpower input, then the contract is an engaged salvage contract, not the salvage contract provided for in the aforementioned international convention and the Maritime Law of China.

2. Where the International Convention on Salvage 1989 and the Maritime Law of China have no specific provisions on engaged salvage contracts, the relevant provisions of the Contract Law of China may be applied to determine the rights and obligations of the parties.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 8 and Article 107 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China
Article 179 of the Maritime Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

The Nanhai Rescue Bureau of the Ministry of Transport (hereinafter referred to as Nanhai Rescue Bureau) alleged: After the M/V "Agios Georgios" ran aground in the Qiongzhou Strait, Nanhai Rescue Bureau was commissioned by Archangelos Investments Inc. (hereinafter referred to as Investments Inc.) to provide services such as salvage, transportation, and standby, but Investments Inc. never paid the salvage fees. The court was requested to order Investments Inc. and the Shanghai Representative Office of Hong Kong Anda Ousen Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Shanghai Representative Office) to jointly pay the salvage fees of RMB 7,240,998.24 and interest.

The court found after trial: The M/V "Agios Georgios," owned by Investments Inc., is a Greek-flagged oil tanker carrying 54,580 tons of Cabinda crude oil. Around 05:00 hours on August 12, 2011, it ran aground near the North Channel of the Qiongzhou Strait. The vessel and its cargo were in peril, seriously threatening the safety of the marine environment. After the incident, Investments Inc. immediately authorized the Shanghai Representative Office to send an urgent email to Nanhai Rescue Bureau regarding the grounding of the M/V "Agios Georgios," requesting Nanhai Rescue Bureau to arrange for two tugs for salvage based on its experience, and indicating agreement with Nanhai Rescue Bureau's quotation.

At 20:40 hours on August 12, the Shanghai Representative Office submitted a power of attorney to Nanhai Rescue Bureau via email, commissioning Nanhai Rescue Bureau to dispatch the tugs "Nanhai Jiu 116" and "Nanhai Jiu 101" to the scene to assist in refloating the M/V "Agios Georgios". It promised to pay the fees at a rate of RMB 3.2 per horsepower-hour, regardless of whether the refloating was successful or not. The billing period would commence from when the tugs started their engines at their respective standby points and end when the Shanghai Representative Office notified the completion of the task and the tugs returned to their original standby points. The "Nanhai Jiu 116" and "Nanhai Jiu 101" were only responsible for towing operations, and Nanhai Rescue Bureau would not be liable for any incidents during the refloating operation of the M/V "Agios Georgios". Additionally, a team of divers was requested to be sent to inspect the M/V "Agios Georgios", with the fee structure being: land mobilization fee of RMB 10,000; water transport fee of RMB 55,000; operation fee of RMB 40,000 per 8-hour period, with the billing period commencing from when the divers boarded the transport vessel and ending when they disembarked ashore after completing the operation. On August 13, Investments Inc. also requested to charter the tug "Nanhai Jiu 201" to transport two of its representatives from Haikou to the M/V "Agios Georgios". Nanhai Rescue Bureau sent an email to the Shanghai Representative Office stating that the rate for "Nanhai Jiu 201" was RMB 1.5 per horsepower-hour, with the total fee calculated based on the charter period.

Meanwhile, to prevent the dangerous situation from worsening and causing marine pollution, the Zhanjiang Maritime Safety Administration decided to implement compulsory lightering and refloating measures for the M/V "Agios Georgios". Arranged by the Zhanjiang Maritime Safety Administration, the M/V "Agios Georgios" successfully refloated on the high tide on August 18 and subsequently arrived safely at its destination port of Qinzhou, Guangxi.

The actual salvage operations carried out by Nanhai Rescue Bureau were as follows:

The tug "Nanhai Jiu 116", owned by Nanhai Rescue Bureau, had a gross tonnage of 3,681 and a total power of 9,000 kilowatts (12,240 hp). After arriving at the incident scene, it stood by the M/V "Agios Georgios" as per Investments Inc.'s instructions, working for a total of 155.58 hours.

The tug "Nanhai Jiu 101", owned by Nanhai Rescue Bureau, had a gross tonnage of 4,091 and a total power of 13,860 kilowatts (18,850 hp). This tug returned before reaching the incident scene. Nanhai Rescue Bureau claimed its working time totaled 13.58 hours.

The tug "Nanhai Jiu 201", owned by Nanhai Rescue Bureau, had a gross tonnage of 552 and a total power of 4,480 kilowatts (6,093 hp). On August 13, it transported two shipowner representatives to the grounded vessel, working for 7.83 hours. On August 16, it transported relevant personnel and equipment to the grounded vessel, working for 7.75 hours. On August 18, it transported relevant personnel and luggage to the lightering vessel, working for 8.83 hours. The divers did not actually perform underwater operations and worked for 8 hours.

It was also found that the salved value of the vessel involved was USD 30,531,856, and the salved value of the cargo was USD 48,053,870. The salved value of the vessel accounted for 38.85% of the total salved value.

Judgment

The Guangzhou Maritime Court, on March 28, 2014, rendered Civil Judgment (2012) Guang Haifa Chu Zi No. 898: 1. Investments Inc. shall pay Nanhai Rescue Bureau a salvage reward of RMB 6,592,913.58 plus interest; 2. Dismissed Nanhai Rescue Bureau's other claims. Investments Inc. appealed against the first-instance judgment. The Guangdong Higher People's Court, on June 16, 2015, rendered Civil Judgment (2014) Yue Gao Fa Min Si Zhong Zi No. 117: 1. Set aside Civil Judgment (2012) Guang Haifa Chu Zi No. 898 of the Guangzhou Maritime Court; 2. Investments Inc. shall pay Nanhai Rescue Bureau a salvage reward of RMB 2,561,346.93 plus interest; 3. Dismissed Nanhai Rescue Bureau's other claims. Nanhai Rescue Bureau, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied for retrial. The Supreme People's Court, on July 7, 2016, rendered Civil Judgment (2016) Zui Gao Fa Min Zai No. 61: 1. Set aside Civil Judgment (2014) Yue Gao Fa Min Si Zhong Zi No. 117 of the Guangdong Higher People's Court; 2. Affirmed Civil Judgment (2012) Guang Haifa Chu Zi No. 898 of the Guangzhou Maritime Court.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that this case is a dispute over a marine salvage contract. The People's Republic of China is a party to the International Convention on Salvage 1989 (hereinafter referred to as the Salvage Convention), and the principles established by the Salvage Convention should be followed in this case. As Investments Inc. is a Greek company and the M/V "Agios Georgios" is a Greek-flagged tanker, this case involves foreign elements. All parties to the litigation uniformly chose to apply the laws of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 3 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, the laws of the People's Republic of China apply to the adjudication of this case. The Maritime Law of China, as a special law governing maritime transport relations and ship relations, shall apply preferentially. Matters not provided for in the Maritime Law shall be governed by the relevant provisions of the Contract Law of China and other relevant laws.

Marine salvage is a traditional international maritime legal institution, and the Salvage Convention and the Maritime Law of China have specific provisions on this matter. Article 12 of the Salvage Convention and Article 179 of the Maritime Law stipulate the payment principle of "no cure, no pay" for salvage rewards. Article 13 of the Salvage Convention and Articles 180 and 183 of the Maritime Law further provide for the criteria for assessing the reward and its specific apportionment based on this principle. These provisions are specific stipulations for marine salvage contracts where the parties determine the salvage reward based on the "no cure, no pay" principle. At the same time, both the Salvage Convention and the Maritime Law of China allow the parties to agree otherwise on the determination of the salvage reward. Therefore, in addition to the "no cure, no pay" salvage contracts stipulated in the Salvage Convention and the Maritime Law of China, engaged salvage contracts can also be formed based on the parties' agreement.

According to the facts established in this case, Investments Inc. and Nanhai Rescue Bureau, after thorough negotiation, explicitly agreed that Investments Inc. would pay the reward regardless of whether the salvage was successful, and that Nanhai Rescue Bureau would not be liable for any incidents during the refloating operation of the M/V "Agios Georgios". According to this agreement, whether Nanhai Rescue Bureau obtained its salvage reward was not directly related to the actual effectiveness of the salvage operation. Furthermore, the calculation of the salvage reward was based on pre-agreed fixed rates and fees, such as the salvage vessel's horsepower-hour and manpower input, and had no connection with the value of the salved property. Therefore, the salvage contract involved in this case is not a "no cure, no pay" salvage contract as defined by the Salvage Convention and the Maritime Law of China, but rather an engaged salvage contract.

Regarding the conditions and standards for the payment of reward under an engaged salvage contract, the Salvage Convention and the Maritime Law of China do not have specific provisions. The courts of first and second instance, by adjusting the fixed rates agreed upon in the engaged salvage contract based on the factors stipulated in Article 180 of the Maritime Law, committed an error in the application of law. This case should be governed and determined by the relevant provisions of the Contract Law of China. It is not improper for Nanhai Rescue Bureau to demand full payment of the agreed salvage reward from Investments Inc. based on the contract concluded between them.

In summary, the second-instance court, using the salvage reward amount determined in the first-instance judgment as the base and applying the Maritime Law, ordered Investments Inc. to pay the salvage reward in proportion to the salved value of the vessel relative to the total salved property value. This application of law and the resulting outcome were erroneous and should be corrected. The first-instance judgment also erred in the application of law, but given that its adjustment of relevant rates was based on the parties' contractual agreement, and Nanhai Rescue Bureau did not raise objections by exercising its relevant litigation rights, the outcome of the first-instance judgment could be affirmed.

(Judges of the effective judgment: He Rong, Zhang Yongjian, Wang Shumei, Yu Xiaohan, Guo Zaiyu)

Guiding Case No. 111

China Construction Bank Corporation,
Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch v.
Guangdong Blue Energy Development Co., Ltd., et al.
— dispute over letter of credit issuance

(Discussed and approved by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on February 25, 2019)

Keywords: Civil / letter of credit issuance / bill of lading / true expression of intention / pledge of rights / priority right to receive payment

Ruling Gist

1. Whether a holder of a bill of lading acquires property rights by receiving delivery of the bill of lading, and what type of property rights are acquired, depends on the terms of the contract. When an issuing bank holds a bill of lading based on the contract between itself and the applicant, the court should, considering the characteristics of letter of credit transactions, reasonably interpret the contract involved to determine the true expression of intention of the issuing bank in holding the bill of lading.

2. If an issuing bank has a pledge right over the bill of lading in the documents under the letter of credit and over the goods covered by that bill of lading, the method by which the issuing bank exercises the pledge right over the bill of lading is the same as the method for exercising a pledge right over movable property represented by the goods under the bill of lading. That is, the issuing bank is entitled to priority in receiving payment from the proceeds obtained from the discount, sale, or auction of the goods under the bill of lading.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 71 of the Maritime Law of the People's Republic of China
Article 224 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China
Paragraph 1 of Article 80 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

China Construction Bank Corporation, Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch (hereinafter referred to as CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch) and Guangdong Blue Energy Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Blue Energy Company) signed the "Trade Financing Facility Agreement" and related appendices, including the "Special Agreement on Issuing Letters of Credit", in December 2011. It was agreed that the bank would provide Blue Energy Company with a trade financing facility not exceeding RMB 550 million, including the issuance of usance letters of credit of equivalent value. Guarantors including Huilai Yuedong Electric Power Fuel Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yuedong Electric Power) signed guarantee contracts. In November 2012, Blue Energy Company applied to CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch for the issuance of a usance letter of credit amounting to RMB 85.92 million. To facilitate the issuance of the letter of credit, Blue Energy Company issued a "Trust Receipt" to CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch and signed a "Margin Pledge Contract". The "Trust Receipt" confirmed that, from the date of its issuance, CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch acquired ownership of the documents and goods covered by the aforementioned letter of credit. CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch was the trustor and beneficiary, and Blue Energy Company was the trustee of the trust goods. After the letter of credit was issued, Blue Energy Company imported 164,998 tons of coal. CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch honored the letter of credit and disbursed RMB 84,867,952.27 to Blue Energy Company, which was used by Blue Energy Company to repay the letter of credit advance made by CCB Seoul Branch. After fulfilling its obligations to issue and pay under the letter of credit, CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch obtained the full set of documents, including the bill of lading involved in this case. Due to its deteriorating business condition, Blue Energy Company failed to pay and take up the documents. Therefore, CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch still held the bill of lading and related documents during the trial of this case. The coal covered by the bill of lading was sealed up by the Fangchenggang City Port Area People's Court of Guangxi due to other disputes. CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch filed a lawsuit, requesting the court to order Blue Energy Company to repay the principal amount of the letter of credit advance of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest; to confirm that CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch held ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal under the letter of credit and was entitled to priority in receiving payment for the aforementioned debt under the letter of credit from the proceeds of disposing of this property; and to order Yuedong Electric Power and other guarantors to assume guarantee liability.

Judgment

Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province rendered Civil Judgment (2013) Sui Zhong Fa Jin Min Chu Zi No. 158 on April 21, 2014, supporting the claims of CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch for repayment of principal and interest by Blue Energy Company and for the guarantors to assume corresponding guarantee liability. However, on the ground that trust receipts and the delivery of bills of lading could not be set up against third parties, the court dismissed CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch's claim for confirmation of coal ownership and priority of compensation. Dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch appealed. The Guangdong High People's Court rendered Civil Judgment (2014) Yue Gao Fa Min Er Zhong Zi No. 45 on September 19, 2014, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. Dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court rendered Civil Judgment (2015) Min Ti Zi No. 126 on October 19, 2015, supporting CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch's right to priority of compensation from the proceeds of disposal of the goods corresponding to the bills of lading under the letter of credit involved in the case, and dismissing its claim for ownership of the goods under the relevant bills of lading.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that a bill of lading has the dual attributes of a document of title and a document of ownership, but this does not mean that whoever holds the bill of lading automatically has ownership of the goods under it. For the holder of a bill of lading, whether it can acquire real rights and what type of real rights it can acquire depends on the agreement between the parties. CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch fulfilled its obligations to issue the letter of credit and make payment and obtained the bills of lading under the letter of credit. However, because there was no expression of intention between the parties to transfer ownership of the goods, it cannot be considered that CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch obtained the ownership of the goods under the bills of lading merely by obtaining them. Although the Trust Receipt stipulated that CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch would obtain ownership of the goods and entrust Blue Energy Company to dispose of the goods under the bills of lading, according to the principle of numerus clausus of real rights, this stipulation could not have the effect of a real right because it constituted a security transfer. However, although the agreement on security transfer could not have the effect of a real right, the agreement still had contractual effect. Moreover, the Special Agreement on Issuance of Letter of Credit stipulated that when Blue Energy Company defaulted, CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch had the right to dispose of the documents and goods under the letter of credit. Therefore, according to the holistic interpretation of the contract and the characteristics of letter of credit transactions, the true intention of the parties was to establish a pledge of the bill of lading through its transfer. This case met the two requirements for the establishment of a pledge of rights: a written pledge contract and publicity of real rights. As the holder of the bills of lading, CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch enjoyed the pledge right over the bills of lading. If the pledge right over the bills of lading held by CCB Guangzhou Liwan Sub-branch conflicted with rights that other creditors might have over the goods under the bills of lading, such as a lien or a pledge of chattels, this could be resolved according to law in the execution distribution procedure.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Liu Guixiang, Liu Min, Gao Xiaoli)

Guiding Case No. 112

AST Co., Ltd. v. Application for Establishment of Maritime Liability Limitation Fund

(Discussed and adopted by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on February 25, 2019)

Keywords Civil / Maritime Liability Limitation Fund / Principle of Incident / Single Incident / Multiple Incidents

Ruling Gist

Article 212 of the Maritime Law establishes the principle that limitation of liability for maritime claims adopts the rule of "one incident, one limit; multiple incidents, multiple limits." The key to determining whether there is one incident or multiple incidents is to analyze whether the incidents arose from the same cause. If multiple incidents arise from the same cause and the chain of causation is unbroken, they shall be deemed as one incident. If the chain of causation is interrupted and another incident subsequently occurs, it shall be deemed as a new and independent incident.

Relevant Legal Provision

Article 212 of the Maritime Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

AST Co., Ltd. applied to the Tianjin Maritime Court, stating that its vessel "E-nong" had received claims for damage to aquaculture. For the non-personal injury losses caused by this incident, AST Co., Ltd., as the shipowner of the vessel, applied for the establishment of a maritime liability limitation fund. The liability limit was 422,510 Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) plus interest on that amount from June 5, 2014 until the date the fund was established.

Numerous aquaculture farmers, as interested parties, raised objections, arguing that AST Co., Ltd. should establish separate limitation funds rather than one fund for the entire voyage.

The court found: The owner of the South Korean-flagged vessel "E-nong" was AST Co., Ltd., with a gross tonnage of 2,030 tons. On June 5, 2014, while sailing from Qinhuangdao to Tianjin Port for loading, the "E-nong" entered an aquaculture area in the sea area of Changli County and Leting County, Hebei Province, causing losses to the relevant aquaculture farmers.

It was further found that at the time of the damage incident, the "E-nong" was using British Admiralty Chart No. 1249, which indicated that aquaculture areas had been established in the sea area where the damage incident occurred and delineated the scope of the aquaculture areas. The pre-set course of the vessel for the voyage in question crossed this aquaculture area.

It was also found that the aquaculture areas of Guo Jinwu and Liu Haizhong were approximately 500 meters apart, with a sailing time of about 2 minutes; the aquaculture areas of Liu Haizhong and Li Weiguo et al. were approximately 9,000 meters apart, with a sailing time of about 30 minutes.

Judgment

The Tianjin Maritime Court rendered Civil Ruling (2014) Jin Hai Fa Xian Zi No. 1 on November 10, 2014: 1. Approval of the application of AST Co., Ltd. for the establishment of a maritime liability limitation fund. 2. The amount of the maritime liability limitation fund was 422,510 SDRs plus interest (interest calculated from June 5, 2014 until the date the fund was established, at the one-year benchmark lending rate for financial institutions determined by the People's Bank of China for the corresponding period). 3. AST Co., Ltd. was to establish the maritime liability limitation fund in Renminbi or with security acceptable to the court within three days from the effective date of the ruling (the Renminbi amount of the fund to be calculated based on the conversion method of SDRs to Renminbi on the effective date of this ruling). Failure to establish the fund within the time limit would be treated as automatic withdrawal of the application. Guo Jinwu and Liu Haizhong, dissatisfied with the first-instance ruling, appealed to the Tianjin High People's Court. The Tianjin High People's Court rendered Civil Ruling (2015) Jin Gao Min Si Zhong Zi No. 10 on January 19, 2015, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original ruling. Guo Jinwu, Liu Haizhong, Li Weiguo, Zhao Laijun, Qi Yongping, Li Jianyong, and Qi Xiukui, dissatisfied with the second-instance ruling, applied for retrial. The Supreme People's Court rendered Civil Ruling (2015) Min Shen Zi No. 853 on August 10, 2015, deciding to retry the case, and rendered Civil Ruling (2015) Min Ti Zi No. 151 on September 29, 2015: 1. Revocation of Civil Ruling (2015) Jin Gao Min Si Zhong Zi No. 10 of the Tianjin High People's Court. 2. Revocation of Civil Ruling (2014) Jin Hai Fa Xian Zi No. 1 of the Tianjin Maritime Court. 3. Dismissal of AST Co., Ltd.'s application for the establishment of a maritime liability limitation fund.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that Article 212 of the Maritime Law establishes the principle of incident for maritime liability limitation, i.e., "one incident, one limit; multiple incidents, multiple limits." The key to determining whether there is one incident or multiple incidents is to analyze whether the two incidents arose from the same cause. If multiple incidents arise from the same cause but the chain of causation is unbroken, they shall be deemed as one incident. If the chain of causation is interrupted and a new cause intervenes, the new cause and the new incident form a new causal relationship, constituting a new and independent incident. In this case, the British Admiralty Chart used by the "E-nong" clearly marked the scope of the aquaculture area, yet the crew set the course into the aquaculture area, which itself constituted gross negligence. When a vessel anticipates that the sea area it will pass through may contain large-scale aquaculture areas, it should strengthen its lookout obligation to ensure navigational safety and avoid colliding with aquaculture areas and causing losses. According to the vessel's navigation trajectory, it actually entered the aquaculture area operated by Guo Jinwu. Given that the damage incident occurred at noon with no nighttime visual impairment, if the crew had diligently performed their lookout and navigation duties, they should have noticed the presence of floating buoys for aquaculture on the sea surface. Given the evidence from the Changli County Oceanic Bureau proving actual damage to Guo Jinwu, it could be presumed that the crew failed to fulfill their diligent lookout obligation, leading to the first tort. According to the navigation trajectory, the vessel subsequently entered Liu Haizhong's aquaculture area. Since Guo Jinwu's and Liu Haizhong's aquaculture areas were adjacent, about 500 meters apart, based on the inertia of the vessel's movement and the laws of vessel maneuverability, the vessel could not take reasonable measures to avoid Liu Haizhong's aquaculture area under the circumstances, resulting in the second tort. Analyzing the cause, both instances of damage resulted from the crew's negligence in lookout before the vessel entered Guo Jinwu's aquaculture area, constituting the same cause, and the chain of causation was not interrupted. Therefore, the two torts should be deemed as one incident. After leaving Liu Haizhong's aquaculture area and entering open waters, the vessel sailed approximately 9,000 meters for about half an hour before entering the aquaculture area of Li Weiguo et al. and causing further damage. Before entering the aquaculture area of Li Weiguo et al., the crew should have had sufficient time to adjust from their negligent psychological state. Moreover, knowing that there were still aquaculture areas ahead on the course, they should have strengthened their lookout obligation to avoid causing further damage. The vessel clearly failed to exercise prudent navigation, leading to the second damage incident. There was no connection between the two incidents, either temporally or subjectively. The occurrence of the second incident was not a natural continuation of the first; there was no causal relationship between the two incidents. AST Co., Ltd.'s argument that the crew's psychological state of erroneous entry remained unchanged throughout the entire process and that the chain of causation was unbroken could not be sustained. Although both incidents arose from a "cause of the same nature," namely the crew's negligent navigation, they did not arise from the "same cause" that led to both incidents. According to the principle of "one incident, one limit," the vessel should establish separate liability limitation funds for each of the two incidents. The courts of first and second instance failed to comprehensively examine the location of the aquaculture areas, the causal relationship between the two incidents, and the subjective state of the parties. Their determination that the vessel caused only one incident and the permission to establish a single fund was erroneous and should be corrected according to law.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Wang Shumei, Fu Xiaoqiang, Huang Xiwu)
